transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-12
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~65 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Mills (Redwood AE), Priya Kaur (Redwood SE), Alex Kim (Redwood Product), Miguel Santos (BlueWave CTO), Rhea Patel (BlueWave ML Eng), Samir Iqbal (BlueWave Infra)
Shared artifacts: Redwood long-context perf spreadsheet (drive link), console-demo deck (slides link), Optimize-recommendations.pdf (also shared)

Summary: quick product walkthrough focused on edge cases: sustained high TPS, very long-context inputs (32k-64k tokens), streaming backpressure and client timeouts. Demonstrated Redwood API behavior, Console observability, and Optimize suggestions plus how Dedicated/Private options change guarantees.

Topics covered: long context handling; KV / prefix caching; batching and shaping requests at high TPS; streaming backpressure and chunking; request timeouts and retry/fallback policies; autoscaling and Dedicated capacity; logging/traceability in Console.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I think we have about an hour, we wanted to run through a tight demo that focuses on a few edge cases you mentioned in the questionnaire — long context, high TPS, streaming backpressure and timeouts. Priya will drive the technical bits.
[00:22] Miguel: thanks, Jordan. yeah we run long transcripts with meeting notes, sometimes up to 50k tokens, and we have bursts to 1.2k requests per second in peak times, so really curious about tail latencies and how you handle streaming when the client side disconnects.
[00:40] Priya: great, that aligns with what we saw in the pre-call notes. quick caveat: some of the product names in my slides are slightly compressed by the export so you might see "Redwood Opti-mize" in places, please ignore the typo. I'll start with a short architecture sketch then demo live calls.
[01:05] Priya: first, long-context: our runtime supports models with extended kv cache and efficient attention kernels. for practical terms what we do is twofold: a) smart prefix caching so repeated history doesn't re-execute the whole forward pass and b) chunked context streaming where we keep only the active window in GPU memory while preserving kv pointers on host, then swap as needed.
[01:30] Rhea: when you say "chunked context streaming", do you mean you actually evict tokens out of GPU KV and then reload on demand? what's the penalty for that in p99?
[01:45] Priya: yes evict/reload. penalty depends on sequence length and model; for our 32k->64k tests we've seen added latency in the 15-50ms range for warm cache reloads; cold reloads can spike higher — but this is where batching and prefetch help. we showed a graph in the spreadsheet. (link).
[02:12] Samir: what's the memory footprint on a 4090-class vs an A100? we run on mixed infra.
[02:20] Priya: good call — on A100 we keep more of the working set resident and see fewer evictions; on 4090-class cards you get more evictions and more host transfers. our runtime has heuristics to pick kernel paths, e.g., flash-attn vs standard, and will prefer quantized kernels if you select that profile in Console.
[02:50] Miguel: latency tradeoffs are acceptable if we keep predictable tail SLOs. how do you protect against traffic surges? we don't want the model to go OOM or to see high queue times.
[03:03] Jordan: this is a pain point for customers. two levers — Dedicated pools with reserved capacity (great for predictable p95), and autoscaling policies with burst capacity. also we have smart routing to fallback to smaller quantized variants when the queue grows.
[03:20] Priya: demo time — I'm going to run three live calls: 1) a 64k token prompt where we show prefix cache hits and a deliberate mid-stream evict, 2) sustained high TPS run at 1k rps for a short window to show batching and latency distribution, 3) streaming backpressure scenario where I kill the client connection to observe server behavior.
[03:45] [screen share starts, console visible; some noise, unclear slide label says "EdgecasePlaybook_v2.pdf"]
[04:05] Priya: first call, POST to /v1/generate with model=rw-64k-test (note: internal test variant), we attach debug trace header. request payload is a concatenation of historical messages ~64k tokens.
[04:30] [beep] Speaker 1: (mutter) oh wow that's huge.
[04:35] Priya: streaming begins — you'll see chunked updates in about 200ms, because we stream tokens back as they're generated. in this run we purposely have a prefix cache hit rate of 85% so the initial response is faster.
[05:00] Rhea: I'm seeing partial transcripts in Console trace, are those the incremental deltas?
[05:05] Priya: yes, the Console shows incremental deltas with token counts and micro-latencies. note the incremental chunks are small (200-400 tokens) to keep memory pressure low.
[05:30] Miguel: what's the maximum request size you allow on hosted API? and what's the behavior if a client tries to send 200k tokens?
[05:42] Jordan: hosted API enforces request size limits — currently 80k tokens for the catalog variant, but dedicated/private can be configured higher with explicit runbook and testing. for 200k tokens we'd recommend chunking upstream or a streaming upload pattern to avoid a single huge call.
[06:05] Priya: next, high TPS test. I'm using our load harness to push 1.2k rps for 90s against a model family and measure observed p50/p95/p99. starting now.
[06:20] [synthetic load noise, console graphs update rapidly]
[06:40] Priya: graph shows p50 ~ 40ms, p95 ~ 120ms, p99 ~ 400-600ms depending on batching alignment. we intentionally tuned batching window to 8-12ms; tightening reduces latency but lowers throughput. you can change that in Optimize to meet cost vs latency goals.
[07:05] Samir: do you support backpressure signals so client-side queues can slow down? our infra uses envoy/passthrough and we need graceful 429s or HTTP/2 flow control hooks.
[07:18] Priya: we emit explicit 429 when queue depth surpasses a threshold, and also include a Retry-After header. for streaming we support chunked transfer signals and if the client read buffer is slow we'll throttle encoding speed and may apply server-side buffer backpressure which is visible in Console as "streaming stalls" events.
[07:45] Miguel: so if the client disconnects mid-stream what happens to billing and state?
[07:52] Jordan: billing is per-token produced and per-embedding unit; if you disconnect, you are billed for tokens generated up to the point of disconnection. state-wise — for hosted we garbage collect KV state after a configurable TTL unless you pin the session with a session-id on Dedicated/Private where you can keep it longer.
[08:15] Priya: now I'll intentionally drop the client socket on a streaming call.
[08:22] [client socket killed; server logs show aborted stream]
[08:30] Priya: server records an aborted stream event; if you have automatic retry policy we can pick up from last acknowledged token if you use idempotent streaming checkpointing (we demonstrated with a sample client in the repo). note there's a small gap because the model's generation isn't cached at token granularity unless you checkpoint.
[09:00] Rhea: what's the guidance around checkpointing for long-running sessions — do we need to do manual checkpoints or can Redwood manage session resumptions?
[09:12] Priya: we provide session checkpoint SDKs for common languages; Redwood will manage KV handles and resume on a new call if you pass the session id and last-ack token. there are limits on how far back you can resume cheaply (we recommend checkpoints every ~2k tokens for very long runs).
[09:40] Alex (Product): i want to add that Optimize will recommend checkpoint cadence based on observed token churn; it can suggest every-n tokens and a cost tradeoff.
[10:00] Miguel: relatedly, how do you surface cost spikes in Console? we need alerting for when quantization fallback or autoscale bumps costs unexpectedly.
[10:10] Jordan: Console has token-level cost breakdowns and alerting rules. you can create a cost alert when a route or model exceeds a cost-per-minute threshold. for dedicated customers we can also push anomaly alerts via webhook.
[10:35] Priya: going back to timeouts — most customer side timeouts are 30s; if a streaming call doesn't emit data within that window the client may drop; we recommend 60s read timeout for long-generation calls or a keepalive ping. also, server-side we have request-level timeouts and a graceful cancellation path so downstream compute is freed quickly.
[11:00] Samir: do you surface the exact point-of-cancellation in trace? we need to reconcile what the app saw vs what the server completed for debugging.
[11:08] Priya: yes, Console traces will show last emitted token index, the cancellation time, and the server-side cost. it's in the request detail pane under "stream events".
[11:30] Miguel: what about eventual consistency in logs if we have private deployment with offline islands? we have air-gapped subnets.
[11:40] Jordan: Private deployment supports on-prem or VPC with optional async log shipping. if air-gapped, logs can be retained locally and pulled via secure export. audit logs and KMS integration are supported — we showed an example SAML/SSO integration in the pre-call doc.
[12:05] Priya: next, a quick demo of Optimize recommendations. I'll load a sample trace and have Optimize propose batching window, quant profile and a fallback policy to keep p95 under 200ms while minimizing cost.
[12:25] [Optimize panel opens]
[12:30] Priya: Optimize suggests smaller batch window for small requests and larger for big ones, plus a two-tier fallback: primary model rw-32b-quant -> fallback rw-8b-quant if queue > 60%. it also picks a prefetch policy for KV evictions to avoid cold reload spikes.
[12:55] Rhea: how fine grained are rollout policies? can we do percent-based canaries for production?
[13:05] Jordan: yes, console supports canary rollouts by percent, by region, by customer segment; you can define automatic fallback to a safe variant if error rates or latencies exceed thresholds.
[13:30] Miguel: let's talk SLOs — we require 99.9% availability and p95 latency under 250ms for a specific route. how do you guarantee that?
[13:40] Jordan: for hosted API we have SLAs for uptime; for latency-sensitive workloads we recommend Dedicated with reserved capacity or hybrid routed to Dedicated in burst windows. we can also set circuit breakers and auto-fallback to cached responses for non-critical reads.
[14:10] Priya: i want to call out one nuance — streaming backpressure with HTTP/2 multiplexing can cause head-of-line issues on some proxies. we recommend using gRPC or dedicated connections for heavy streaming workloads to avoid muxing stalls.
[14:35] Samir: our platform uses envoy — anything special to configure?
[14:40] Priya: tune idle timeouts, increase http2 concurrent stream limits, and ensure upstream read buffer sizes are large. we can share a perf tuning guide.
[15:05] Miguel: curious about failure modes. if a model OOMs mid-generation at p99 scale, what's the graceful behavior? do you get a partial output or full abort?
[15:16] Priya: OOM typically triggers an abort; we surface partial outputs if tokens were streamed before the crash. for long runs you should enable checkpointing and small chunked streaming so client sees incremental progress. also Optimize can recommend quantization/profiles to reduce OOM frequency.
[15:45] [pause — attendees sipping coffee, minor crosstalk]
[16:05] Priya: i'm going to show a recorded perf run from the spreadsheet where we simulated 2k rps for 30s to illustrate autoscale behavior and queue growth.
[16:25] [playback] Priya: note the blue line is queue depth, orange is scaling events. we saw a 30s scale-up delay to add more GPUs on cloud-provider autoscale; Dedicated with reserved headroom avoids that delay.
[16:50] Miguel: what's the minimum reservation for Dedicated to keep p99 under 800ms at our traffic? we've sent you the p95/p99 numbers in the pre-call doc.
[17:00] Jordan: rough ballpark from the numbers you shared: a 4-GPU reserve on A100-class should keep p99 within target for your baseline with a 2x burst reserve. we'll put exact sizing in the follow-up spreadsheet.
[17:25] Rhea: a practical question — for local dev and integration tests we want deterministic behavior. any guidance to avoid flakey tests due to batching heuristics?
[17:40] Priya: yes — use a deterministic local SDK flag to disable batching and set a fixed seed for generation and you get consistent latencies and outputs. for CI you might use a small model variant with the same code path.
[18:05] Miguel: back to billing — in a streaming abort case you charge for tokens produced but not acknowledged, can you provide a reconciliation log?
[18:15] Jordan: yes Console has request-level billing entries; you can cross-reference and we'll provide a CSV export for audits.
[18:30] [a brief side tangent about compliance and SOC2]
[19:05] Priya: final demo: simulate slow client read buffer to show streaming stalls. starting now.
[19:20] [console shows "streaming stalls" event, per-chunk latencies climb]
[19:35] Priya: stalls are visible as spikes in per-chunk latency and we throttle encode speed; Optimize suggests reducing chunk size and enabling early flush for your client lib to reduce buffer bloat.
[20:01] Samir: is there an SDK knob to auto-detect slow readers?
[20:08] Priya: yes, SDK exposes a callback when backpressure exceeds threshold; we also emit metrics you can alert on.
[20:30] Miguel: ok last area — retries. if we get transient 503s under high load, what's the recommended client retry strategy?
[20:42] Priya: exponential backoff with jitter, but cap retries for streaming calls; for idempotent generates you can retry from last checkpoint. also respect 429 Retry-After. Optimize can produce recommended retry windows from historical traces.
[21:05] [longer Q&A for next ~30 minutes — distilled highlights below] 
[21:10] Rhea: can Redwood provide a test harness that we can run in our VPC to simulate our exact network conditions?
[21:18] Jordan: yes, we have a perf kit you can run in VPC; for Private deployments we can co-run perf with your team. we'll attach the perf kit in the follow-up.
[21:40] Samir: security checklist — SAML/SSO, KMS, audit logs, PCI-ish concerns. how much of that is off-the-shelf in Private?
[21:55] Jordan: Private includes SAML/SSO integration, KMS/HSM options, and audit logging. for specific compliance we can map controls and provide gap analysis.
[22:20] Miguel: timeline question — if we sign POC this quarter how quickly can we run a Dedicated pilot?
[22:30] Jordan: we typically stand up a Dedicated pilot in 2-3 weeks once contract and infra access are ready. Private on-prem can take longer — depends on your security approvals.
[22:50] Priya: quick note — we'll need sample payloads and a perf window. Samir, you mentioned a 4-hour window on 2/25 in the notes?
[23:00] Samir: yes 2/25 02:00-06:00 UTC works for us.
[23:10] Jordan: perfect.
[23:18] [closing recap] Jordan: recap: Priya will run the 64k and 64k+ checkpoint perf runs and share the spreadsheet — due 2/19; Jordan will send Dedicated pricing and console recording — due 2/16; Samir will provide exact p95/p99 traces and confirm perf window — due 2/17; BlueWave to confirm 2/25 perf window.
[23:45] Miguel: thanks — this was helpful; main ask is reproducible perf under our env and a clear pilot plan.
[24:00] Jordan: we'll follow up with a runbook and test harness; expect an email with calendar invites and links. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription quality and artifacts: occasional mislabels (Speaker 1), minor garbling of product names (Opti-mize), and some truncation in the screen-share timestamps. Console links and spreadsheet referenced above will be attached to CRM.
